title: What If a Bomber Dropped Two H-Bombs on North Carolina? In 1961 One Did

scenes.text: What if a B-52 dropped two hydrogen bombs on North Carolina? In 1961, one did.
Past midnight, January 24th, a fuel-leaking B-52 broke apart over Goldsboro. Two hydrogen bombs fell out, each around 250 Hiroshimas.
Bomb one's parachute opened. It was found hanging from a tree, nose in the dirt, almost undamaged.
Its arming sequence had started. Three of four safety switches had tripped. One low-voltage switch held.
Bomb two hit a muddy field at over 700 miles an hour and shattered. Crews dug 50 feet. Flooding stopped them.
Its uranium stage is still down there, about 180 feet deep. The Air Force bought the digging rights. It is still farmland.

description:
What if a bomber dropped two hydrogen bombs on North Carolina? On the night of 23 to 24 January 1961 a B-52 broke apart in mid-air near Goldsboro and both of its Mark 39 bombs, about 3.8 megatons each, fell to earth. Three of the eight crew died.
One bomb parachuted into a tree with three of its four arming safety devices tripped; a 1969 Sandia memo, declassified in 2013, said one low-voltage switch stood between the US and a major catastrophe. The other hit a field at over 700 mph; its secondary stage was never recovered and is calculated to lie about 180 feet down.
What should we run through next?
first_comment: Radiation tests at the site have never found anything above background. Would you farm that field? Drop your own what-if below.
